newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish hostages in Yemen said free, not confirmed.
newsitem.headline: Polish hostages in Yemen said free, not confirmed.

text.p: Five Polish tourists held hostage by tribesmen in Yemen have been freed, Poland's foreign ministry quoted Yemeni authorities as saying on Tuesday.
"Yemen's foreign and interior ministries say they are already free," Przemyslaw Antoniewicz, deputy head of the ministry's press office, told Reuters.
He added that the report had yet to be confirmed by Polish diplomats on the spot and that Poland's ambassador in Yemen had not yet personally seen the hostages.
A Polish diplomat in Yemen said his embassy did not have firm information that the crisis was over.
"We have not received reliable information about a successful completion of negotiations with the tribesmen," Stanislaw Smolen, Poland's consul in Sanaa, told Reuters.
"We cannot say that there has been a failure or success or and end to the crisis," he said.

The three men and two women aged between 50 and 64 were kidnapped on their way to archaeological sites last week by members of the Al al-Masni tribe in the Khawlan area about 65 km (40 miles) east of the capital Sanaa.
Yemen authorities have been in negotiations with the kidnappers to secure the hostages' release.
Smolen said the talks had reportedly resumed at 4 p.m. (1300 GMT) but that the Polish mission had been receiving conflicting information from Yemen authorities.
On Friday, the tribesmen fired grenades at military forces surrounding them, killing three soldiers and wounding five.

Tribes in Yemen with grievances against the government or foreign oil firms have in recent years kidnapped foreigners to use in bargaining with the authorities, often over land or water issues or requests for aid.
Polish officials have declined to name the hostages.
A leading member of a club devoted to exotic foreign travel told Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper she believed they were from the Polish Explorers' Society.

Biologist Zofia Sikorska-Piwowska said their reported ages and sexes fitted those of five society members who had left on December 10 for a tour of Yemen, Ethiopia and Sudan and who included a freelance journalist and a couple of physicists.
